extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and working stand-up comedians (open-mic performers and professional comics)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, stage-focused process for generating, testing, revising, and polishing stand-up jokes and set material for open mics and club performances. Emphasizes capturing real moments, forming clear premises, drafting multiple punchlines, stage-testing, and integrating polished bits into a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture (always have a notebook/phone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notebook (or phone) ALWAYS on you. Capture the moment something annoys, confuses, or amuses you — without trying to make it funny yet. Capture the EMOTION first, not the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a constant capture system so you don't rely on memory. Focus on the felt emotion or experience as raw material; avoid forcing a punchline at this stage. Anti-pattern: trying to craft the perfect joke immediately and losing the authentic emotional kernel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular review and premise extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a week, review captures. For each, write down: 'What I really mean is...' That sentence is your premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a single-sentence premise from each captured moment to clarify the idea you'll write from. This acts as the spine of the joke and helps you avoid wandering. Example prompt: 'What I really mean is...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting: start with the premise and generate multiple punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the premise as the FIRST line. (You'll cut it later, but it focuses the writing.) Write five different punchlines for the same premise. Pick the funniest two. Combine the second-funniest as a tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the premise as a focal anchor while drafting—keeping it first helps focus thought even if it's removed later. Produce many punchline variations (recommendation: five) to explore directions; select and pair the best and second-best lines to create primary punch and tag. Anti-pattern: settling on the first punchline or failing to generate alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-test jokes exactly as written
rubrics_metrics.description: Try the joke at an open mic exactly as written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the material as drafted to get a clean test of whether the writing works. Treat the first stage appearances as data-gathering, not final performance. Avoid improvising different phrasings on the first tests if you want comparable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe audience response and rewrite to feature what worked
rubrics_metrics.description: Note what the audience laughed at — sometimes a throwaway line gets the laugh, not the punch. Rewrite to feature whatever actually worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be empirical: if a side line or a different beat gets the response, re-center the joke around that moment. Keep notes after each performance about exact laugh points. Anti-pattern: ignoring audience feedback and forcing the original written punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish after multiple stage attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: After 5+ stage attempts, settle the wording. Build it into your set order — usually pair with thematically adjacent material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only finalize and refine wording after the joke has been trialed across several rooms; then integrate it thoughtfully into your set flow and theme. Recommendation: minimum of five room tests before final polish. Consider sequencing and thematic adjacency for better set cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit on stage, not at the desk
rubrics_metrics.description: They edit on stage, not at the desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer live iterative refinement driven by real audience reaction over solitary desk rewriting. Use performances as the primary editing environment. Anti-pattern: over-polishing in private without sufficient stage data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to throw away most material
rubrics_metrics.description: They throw away 90% of what they write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect high rejection of ideas; view writing as volume work where most drafts are discarded. Maintain productivity rather than clinging to drafts. Scoring note: prolific capture + ruthless culling improves the signal-to-noise of your set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill lines that die repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: They don't fall in love with a line; if it dies three times, it's dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a practical lifespan rule: if a line fails to land across repeated attempts (three failures suggested), remove it. Avoid emotional attachment that wastes stage time. Anti-pattern: repeating a dead line hoping for a different outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and review every set
rubrics_metrics.description: They listen to recordings of every set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record performances and review them to catch details you missed in the moment (timing, audience reaction, pacing). Use recordings to inform rewrites and to identify where laughs actually occur versus where you thought they did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share material with trusted peers for honest feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: They share material with one or two trusted comics for honest feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small, trusted circle for critique to avoid groupthink and to get candid reactions. Choose peers who will be straightforward rather than just supportive. Anti-pattern: broad sharing that dilutes your voice or exposes material prematurely without honest critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin authenticity — comes from a real captured moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it come from a real moment you captured?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a retention/evaluation criterion: prefer material grounded in authentic lived experience or real emotional moments rather than contrived premises. This increases relatability and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear premise under the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it have a clear premise underneath?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke has a coherent underlying idea that can be stated simply (e.g., 'What I really mean is...'). A clear premise helps the audience follow the logic and amplifies the punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation testing — try multiple punchline variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you tried at least three punchline variations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deciding on a final line, experiment with multiple punchlines (page recommends five when drafting; rubric asks for at least three). Use stage tests to compare which variations land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proven landing across rooms (minimum tests)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical criterion for retention: the joke should have landed across multiple different audiences/rooms (recommendation: 5+) before settling wording and integration into a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained performer interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you still interested in saying it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-interest and enthusiasm for the material matter; if the performer is bored or disengaged, the joke is less likely to feel fresh onstage. This is a viability filter alongside audience data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with overall POV/persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it fit your overall POV / persona?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the joke aligns with your established comedic voice and persona to maintain coherent set identity. Jokes that contradict persona may confuse audiences or reduce set effectiveness.
